sentences.en: Welcome to 'Are you in the mood?'.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Welcome at 'Have you fun?'.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Welkom bij" is a common phrase used to welcome someone to a place or event, where "bij" means "at" or "to."  
• The phrase "Heb je zin?" literally translates to "Do you have fun?" but in practice, it can mean "Are you excited?" or "Are you in the mood?".  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Welkom bij de vergadering." (Welcome to the meeting.)  
  - "Heb je zin om te gaan?" (Are you in the mood to go?)  
  - "Welkom bij ons thuis." (Welcome to our home.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• Welkom bij de cursus! (Welcome to the course!)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch culture, informal greetings like "Heb je zin?" are common in casual settings. It reflects a friendly and inviting atmosphere.

sentences.nl: We gaan weer Nederlandse zinnen oefenen.
Ken je Marieke en Martin nog? — Uit de vorige les? — Marieke is docent Nederlands.
sentences.en: Do you still know Marieke and Martin? — From the previous lesson? — Marieke is a Dutch teacher.
sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Know you Marieke and Martin still? — From the previous lesson? — Marieke is teacher Dutch.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ken je" is an informal way to ask if someone knows someone else, using the verb "kennen" (to know).  
• "Nog" means "still," indicating continuity from the past to the present.  
• "Uit de vorige les" means "from the previous lesson," showing the use of "uit" to indicate origin or source.  
• "Docent Nederlands" directly translates to "teacher Dutch," which is how you structure professions in Dutch. 

Examples:  
• "Ken je mijn broer nog?" (Do you still know my brother?)  
• "Uit de krant heb ik dat nieuws." (I got that news from the newspaper.)  
• "Hij is leraar Engels." (He is an English teacher.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Ken je de weg naar het station nog?" (Do you still know the way to the station?)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, it's common for teachers to be referred to by their first name, especially in less formal educational settings.

sentences.nl: Hij gaat naar de school van Marieke in Rotterdam.

sentences.explanation:
## 1. Literal Translation  
• Here gives Marieke Dutch lesson

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence follows the structure: "Adverb - Verb - Subject - Object," which is common in Dutch for emphasis on the location or time.  
• "Hier" (here) is an adverb of place, indicating where the action takes place.  
• "Geeft" is the third person singular present tense of "geven" (to give).  
• "Nederlandse les" (Dutch lesson) is a compound noun phrase where "Nederlandse" is an adjective modifying "les."  

Extra sentences:  
- "Daar eet hij zijn lunch." (There he eats his lunch.)  
- "Vandaag speelt zij voetbal." (Today she plays soccer.)  
- "Binnen leest Peter een boek." (Inside Peter reads a book.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Op school leert Eva wiskunde." (At school, Eva learns mathematics.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In the Netherlands, learning Dutch is often emphasized for integration, especially for newcomers. Language classes like the one Marieke is giving are common in community centers or schools.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Pedro comes from Spain.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Komt uit" is a common Dutch structure meaning "comes from," indicating origin or source. The verb "komen" is in the present tense and is conjugated for the third person singular, "Pedro."  
• The preposition "uit" is used similarly to "from" in English. It indicates the point of origin.  
• Extra examples:  
  - "Zij komt uit Italië." (She comes from Italy.)  
  - "Wij komen uit Nederland." (We come from the Netherlands.)  
  - "Hij komt uit een klein dorp." (He comes from a small village.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Maria komt uit Portugal." (Maria comes from Portugal.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, mentioning someone's place of origin is a common way to introduce someone or explain a part of their background, similar to many other cultures.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Ulrich is a German.

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• "Ulrich is een Duitser." follows a simple subject-verb-object structure. "Ulrich" is the subject, "is" is the verb, and "een Duitser" is the predicate nominative.  
• The word "Duitser" is a noun meaning "German" (referring to a male person from Germany). In Dutch, nationalities can have gender-specific forms.  
• Example phrases:  
  - "Hij is een Nederlander." (He is a Dutchman.)  
  - "Zij is een Française." (She is a Frenchwoman.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Karin is een Zwitserse." (Karin is a Swiss woman.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• In Dutch, nationalities often have gender-specific endings, such as "-er" for males and "-se" for females, which reflects the language's attention to gender in such contexts.

## 1. Literal Translation  
• Martin, talk Dutch with me!

## 2. Grammar Explanation and Extensions  
• The sentence is an imperative, giving a command or request. In Dutch, imperatives often start with the verb.  
• "Praat" is the imperative form of "praten" (to talk/speak).  
• "Met mij" means "with me", showing accompaniment or interaction.  
• Personal names like "Martin" are often used to direct the command to a specific person.

Examples:  
• "Luister naar mij." (Listen to me.)  
• "Eet je groenten op." (Eat your vegetables up.)  
• "Schrijf je naam op het bord." (Write your name on the board.)

## 3. Create a New Example  
• "Anna, lees het boek met me." (Anna, read the book with me.)

## 4. Culture Note (If there is any)  
• Speaking Dutch in the Netherlands is appreciated when trying to connect with locals, even if your Dutch isn't perfect. It shows effort and respect for the language.
